story.title: Cleanup Efforts Underway After Thanksgiving Storm Disrupts East Coast
story.summary: A Thanksgiving storm has caused significant disruptions across the East Coast, leaving approximately 480,000 homes and businesses without power as of Friday, down from 900,000 the previous day. The storm brought heavy rain and strong winds, leading to travel delays and necessitating water rescues from New York to Virginia. While conditions are improving, some areas remain on alert for potential high-tide flooding.

event_overview.title: About Day Storm
event_overview.subject: Day Storm
event_overview.summary: “Day Storm” refers here to the Midwest-to-Eastern U.S. Thanksgiving storm of November 2026, a strong low-pressure system that developed near the Southeast coast and moved north along the East Coast during the Thanksgiving holiday. It combined heavy rain, damaging winds and coastal flooding in the East with wintry precipitation in parts of the Mid-Mississippi Valley, disrupting travel and public events.

facts.label: Dates
facts.value: The system developed on November 25, 2026, intensified and moved up the East Coast through Thanksgiving on November 26, and continued to produce impacts into November 27.

facts.label: Storm type and track
facts.value: The National Weather Service Weather Prediction Center characterized it as a strong coastal storm: low pressure formed off the Southeast coast and tracked northeastward along the Eastern Seaboard.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Its principal coastal hazards extended from the Carolinas into the Northeast, while associated winter weather affected parts of the Mid-Mississippi Valley, including Missouri.

facts.label: Main hazards
facts.value: Forecast and warning materials identified heavy rain, strong winds, major coastal flooding, beach erosion and some wintry precipitation as the central hazards; coastal flood warnings extended from North Carolina to southern Connecticut at the storm's peak.

facts.label: Notable public-event disruption
facts.value: In New York City, officials postponed the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade from Thanksgiving Day to Saturday, November 28, citing expected high winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows major Thanksgiving-week disruptions, including the parade postponement and flooding and power-outage impacts; it does not aim to document every local forecast, warning, damage report, restoration update or travel disruption caused by the broader storm.

explore_lenses.label: Why were outages and flooding so widespread?
explore_lenses.title: Wind, rain and tides compounded the damage
explore_lenses.summary: The disruption was driven by a coastal storm combining heavy rain, damaging winds and elevated astronomical tides, rather than rainfall alone. Those conditions increased both power-line damage and coastal-road flooding risks.

claims.text: The National Weather Service forecast coastal wind gusts above 50 mph, with gusts above 45 mph possible inland to the I-95 corridor; it said tree damage and power outages were possible.

The Weather Prediction Center said strong onshore winds, high surf and high astronomical tides were expected to produce significant flooding and beach erosion from the Carolinas through the Northeast.
New Jersey’s emergency order cited an elevated risk that wind gusts of 50 to 70 mph—potentially higher on the coast—would cause outages and impede normal public and private operations.

explore_lenses.label: Why can flood danger remain after the rain eases?
explore_lenses.title: High-tide cycles can prolong coastal impacts
explore_lenses.summary: A reduction in rainfall does not immediately end coastal flood risk because water levels can remain elevated through subsequent high tides. This is particularly relevant for low-lying roads, bayside communities and beaches.

claims.text: The National Weather Service said the storm’s biggest coastal concern was flooding caused by the combination of onshore winds, high surf and high astronomical tides, and warned that peak flooding could cut off roadway access in parts of the Virginia Tidewater, Chesapeake and Delaware bays, and southern New Jersey.
On November 27, reporting based on the National Weather Service said coastal flood warnings remained in effect from New Jersey to Virginia even as the storm’s heavy rain was winding down.
New Jersey’s emergency order described repeated tidal-flooding rounds and said high tides could make roads impassable, damage vulnerable structures and isolate some locations.

explore_lenses.label: What should affected communities expect next?
explore_lenses.title: Restoration continues, with residual hazards
explore_lenses.summary: Utilities were restoring service as the outage total declined, but the storm was expected to weaken gradually rather than end immediately. Residents and travelers may still face wind, coastal-flood and transportation effects during the transition.

story_report.summary: A Thanksgiving storm battered the East Coast with heavy rain and strong winds from Virginia to New York, disrupting travel and prompting water rescues. About 480,000 homes and businesses remained without power on Nov. 27, down from roughly 900,000 the day before, as cleanup and restoration efforts continued. Although the heaviest rain was easing, coastal flooding threats remained in place in parts of the region.

sections.heading: Winds Strain Power Infrastructure
sections.body: The National Weather Service forecast coastal wind gusts above 50 mph and possible gusts above 45 mph inland to the I-95 corridor, conditions it said could damage trees and cause power outages. New Jersey’s emergency order cited a risk of gusts between 50 and 70 mph, potentially stronger along the coast, that could disrupt normal public and private operations.

sections.heading: Coastal Flooding Remains Primary Hazard
sections.body: Forecasters said onshore winds, high surf and high astronomical tides could produce significant flooding and beach erosion from the Carolinas through the Northeast. The National Weather Service warned that peak flooding could cut off road access in the Virginia Tidewater, Chesapeake and Delaware bays, and southern New Jersey. Coastal flood warnings remained in effect from New Jersey to Virginia on Nov. 27.

sections.heading: Forecast Calls for Gradual Improvement
sections.body: The Weather Prediction Center projected the storm low to move north toward southeastern Canada by Saturday, while the National Weather Service said additional outages and travel impacts were possible before conditions improved on Sunday. Forecasters advised coastal residents and holiday travelers to monitor National Weather Service forecasts and local officials.

related_stories.title: Kenyan cult leader convicted of manslaughter for 123 deaths, adding to previous murder sentences
related_stories.summary: Paul Mackenzie, the leader of a starvation cult in Kenya, has been found guilty of manslaughter for the deaths of 123 followers. This conviction follows his earlier sentencing to 200 years in prison for the murder of nearly 200 children. Mackenzie has also faced charges related to radicalization and organized criminal activity.

related_stories.title: Allies Condemn Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia, Pledge Support
related_stories.summary: Officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye have condemned recent Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, labeling them as 'heinous.' During discussions in Islamabad, the three nations reaffirmed their commitment to protect Saudi Arabia's security under a defense pact. This collaboration aims to bolster regional stability amid ongoing threats.

related_stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada Upholds Quebec's Ban on Religious Symbols for Public Servants
related_stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada has largely upheld Quebec's Bill 21, which prohibits public servants from wearing religious symbols, including hijabs, turbans, and crosses. The law, enacted in 2019, aims to maintain a secular state, but has faced criticism for potentially infringing on individual rights. Legal challenges were brought forth by various groups, including teachers from different religious backgrounds, who argued that the law violates their fundamental rights.
